newsitem.title: USA: June retail sales up more strongly than expected.
newsitem.headline: June retail sales up more strongly than expected.

text.p: Sales at retail stores picked up more strongly than expected in June following three straight monthly declines, the Commerce Department said on Tuesday, suggesting a potential revival in consumer activity.
Total retail sales increased last month by 0.5 percent to a seasonally adjusted $210.3 billion after a revised 0.3 percent drop in May. A surprising rise in sales by auto dealers boosted June sales.
Excluding new cars, June retail sales were up 0.3 percent after being flat in May.
Last month's sales figures were contrary to Wall Street economists's forecasts for a smaller 0.2 percent rise in overall sales and for a 0.5 percent gain excluding autos.

Major automakers had previously reported lackluster June sales, so the increase reported by the government was not anticipated. The June sales report included a sharp revision to May new-car sales, showing they dropped more sharply -- by 1.2 percent instead of the 0.2 percent reported a month ago.
New cars account for a quarter of total retail sales, so swings in demand strongly affect the overall monthly figures.
Sales of all types of durable goods, from cars to refrigerators and furniture, rose 0.5 percent in June to $85.1 billion after a 0.9 percent fall in May.
Sales of non-durables like food and clothing were up 0.4 percent last month to $125.2 billion after rising 0.1 percent in May.

Sales by general merchandise stores rose 0.8 percent to $27.5 billion following a 0.5 percent gain in May. At apparel stores, clothing sales were flat in June at $9.6 billion after rising 1.2 percent in May.

Industry reports from chain stores, which sell everything from clothing to general merchandise, had already indicated some improvement in business last month, though analysts noted that many stores heavily discounted prices to boost sales.
The June retail sales report may make markets uneasy about a possible pickup in second-half economic activity.

After shooting ahead at a booming 5.9 percent annual rate in the first quarter, economic growth measured by Gross Domestic Product is widely forecast to have slowed to a rate around 2 percent to 2.5 percent in the quarter ended June 30.
Analysts are watching closely for evidence that growth may re-accelerate in the second half, potentially leading the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to restrain expansion.

U.S. central bank policymakers are scheduled to meet again on Aug. 19 to consider interest-rate strategy. The Fed has held rates steady at its past two policysetting sessions amid signs inflation was muted to nonexistent.
There were declines in sales during June for several categories of goods.
Sales of building materials fell 1.2 percent in June to $11.9 billion after a 0.1 percent decline in May.
Sales by food stores fell 0.1 percent to $35.8 billion following a 0.1 percent May rise.
Gasoline service station sales decreased 0.9 percent to $12.7 billion after falling 2 percent in May. But the sales figures may reflect recent declines in gasoline prices.
